Litigation
lĭt-ĭ-gā´shŭn
n. (the carrying on of a lawsuit; contest in a court of law)
Latin litigare, to dispute at law, from lis, a lawsuit, and agere, to drive. Paul's word for the practice among Christians is simply to go to law.

Biblical Definition

Litigation between believers is what Paul confronts at Corinth. He begins with astonishment: “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” (1Co 6:1). He then concedes the case is already lost whoever wins: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” (1Co 6:7). The Lord's counsel runs the same way: “if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also” (Mat 5:40); and, “when thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate… give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him” (Luk 12:58).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines litigation as the act or process of carrying on a suit in a court of law or equity; judicial contest; and litigious as inclined to judicial contest, quarrelsome.

expand to see more

LITIGATION, n. The act or process of carrying on a suit in a court of law or equity for the recovery of a right or claim; a judicial contest.

LITIGIOUS, a. Inclined to judicial contest; given to the practice of contending in law; quarrelsome; contentious; fond of litigation.

2. Disputable; controvertible; subject to contention.

Key Scripture

1Co 6:1 — "Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?"

1Co 6:7 — "Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?"

Mat 5:40 — "And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also."

Luk 12:58 — "When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, as thou art in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him; lest he hale thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and the officer cast thee into prison."

Mat 18:15 — "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."

Modern Corruption

Winning is treated as vindication, and Paul says the lawsuit itself is the defeat.

expand to see more

First Corinthians 6:7 is the sentence that dismantles the whole calculation: there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Not because the plaintiff was wrong about the facts — Paul never examines the merits. The existence of the suit is the failure, and it belongs to both parties and to the congregation that could not settle it. The world is watching brothers in a public dispute over money, and no verdict repairs what that has already said about the gospel they claim.

Then come the two questions the church has never wanted: why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Paul is asking a wronged man to absorb a real loss. That is not naivety about justice — he elsewhere insists on his rights as a citizen, appeals to Caesar, and demands that the magistrates at Philippi come and fetch him out themselves. The distinction is that a believer's own vindication against a brother is the thing he is free to give up, because he has a Judge and a future that make the loss survivable.

The positive instruction is not passivity but process. Verse 5 asks whether there is not a wise man among you who shall be able to judge between his brethren, which assumes the church can and should hear such matters; Matthew 18 gives the escalation, and 1 Timothy 5:19 the evidentiary standard. A congregation with no capacity to settle a dispute between members will drive them to the courts by default. The alternative to litigation is not silence — it is a church that can hear a case.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek krino (G2919), to go to law, judge; krima (G2917), a matter for judgment, a fault; adikeo (G91), to suffer wrong; apostereo (G650), to be defrauded.

expand to see more

Greek krinesthai (G2919) — to go to law, be judged; 1 Corinthians 6:1, 6:6, Matthew 5:40.

Greek hettema (G2275) — a fault, a defeat, coming short; 1 Corinthians 6:7, Romans 11:12.

Greek adikeisthe / apostereisthe (G91, G650) — take wrong / suffer defrauding; 1 Corinthians 6:7.

Usage

"“There is utterly a fault among you” — and the merits are never examined."

"“Why do ye not rather take wrong?” — a real loss, absorbed."

"“Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you?” — the church should hear it."
